To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the preheating temperature affects the thermal gel properties of Alaska pollack surimi, and this is due to myosin denatulation and cross-linking reactions.
the thermal gel properties of Alaska pollack surimi are improved by preheating at 15-35°C, and the mechanism of the improvement involves myosin denatuation and cross-linking reactions.
myosin aggregates as revealed by the urea-soluble myosin and the cross-linking reactions are important in improving thermal properties of surimi gels.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the denaturation of myosin during the preheated process of Alaska pollak salted surimi, and its effect on the thermal gel properties.
the effect of preheating temperature on thermal gel properties of Alaska pollack surimi.

the effect of preheating temperature on myosin denatuation and cross-linking in Alaska pollack salt surimi during its preheating process, and the effect of these changes in myosin on the thermal gel properties of preheat gel and those after heating.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
myosin cross-linkage was the most important factor in improving the thermal gel properties of Alaska pollack surimi.
myosin denatution and aggregation are important factors in determining thermal gel properties of surimi.
the preheating temperature must be below the temperature of the cross-linking of myosin to produce a high-quality thermal gel.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
myosin aggregates formed at 35°C and 15°C, but not at 25°C and 45°C.

preheating at temperatures below the optimum (35°C) for cross-linking reaction would result in the formation of aggregates of myosin, and that these aggregates were important in the improvement in gel properties.
myosin denaturations and cross-linking reactions during preheating were important in determining thermal gel properties of surimi.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the preheating temperature should be selected based on the temperature at which the loss of ureasolubility of salted surimi myosin and the cross-linking of myosin aggregates occur.
preheating at temperatures between 35°C and 45°C was optimal for the formation of a gel that was strong and had a fine structure.
preheating at 35°C is the optimal temperature for improving gel properties.
